gaps.row: Ounces and amounts for regular sized bottles
gaps.fact: The capacity of the common bottles in standard (US fluid) ounces as well as metric: 375 ml about 12.7 oz, 750 ml about 25.4 oz (the Court's 25), 1.5 litre magnum about 50.7 oz. The bottles table is metric only and no stem converts a bottle to ounces; only the chapter's five 5 oz glasses implies 25.

gaps.row: Ounces and amounts for regular sized bottles
gaps.fact: The uncommon sizes in metric and standard: 1 litre (about 33.8 oz), 187 ml (about 6.3 oz) and the jeroboam. The bottles table gives the three in millilitres and litres; no stem in either bank asks the litre, the 187 ml or the jeroboam (s-qxvy3m2u is a service question outside both banks), and no ounce figure appears.

gaps.row: Amount of pours from a standard bottle
gaps.fact: Pours from a standard bottle at the Court's sizes: 2, 4, 5 and 6 oz from 25 oz give 12.5, about 6, 5 and about 4 pours; 60, 118, 148 and 187 ml give 12.5, about 6, about 5 and 4. No stem works in ounces, and the only pour sizes asked are 150 ml and 75 ml.

BTB, revenue, net profit and ullage in its trade sense (wine or beer lost and written off). BTB is never named; revenue and net profit are never defined, though c-j1zp2eyy says gross profit comes before wages and rent; ullage is taught only as the gap under a cork (c-yqxiozm7); spillage is a single word in the chapter's shrinkage list.

Inventory change = beginning inventory minus ending inventory, the step inside cost of goods sold. The chapter gives the full formula and c-eg0a7xci asks what the count feeds, but no stem computes cost of goods sold or the inventory change from opening and closing figures.

gaps.row: Amount of 750ml bottles in a case
gaps.fact: A standard case is 9 litres, twelve 750 ml bottles, and not all cases are twelve: super premium wines come in cases of 6 or 3. Never taught; OWC alone is asked (c-96upusir, in Wine Trade & Aging).

The Court's four way rule: a higher selling price raises margin and a lower one lowers it; a higher product cost lowers margin and a lower one raises it. The chapter and stems work cost percentage against cash, but the plain rule is never stated or asked.

Pour cost starting from case cost (case cost divided by the bottles in the case, then by the pours in the bottle, then over the glass price). Every costing stem starts from a bottle cost; none starts from a case.
Bottles needed = (number of guests x ounces or millilitres per guest) / 25 (ounces in a bottle). No stem works out how many bottles an event needs.

errors.where: js/data-primers.js, PRIMERS Business of the Sommelier, traps: 'Price the glass from the wholesale cost, not from the bottle's list price.'
errors.claim: A by the glass figure is worked from the bottle's wholesale cost and never from its list price.
errors.correction: Keep the wholesale rule as the pricing convention it is (one glass at the bottle's cost), but teach beside it the Court's own BTG costing, which starts from the list price: BTG cost = (bottle list price / 25 oz or 750 ml) x the pour, so a bottle listed at 100 gives a 5 oz glass at 20. As written, the trap tells a candidate to refuse the very input the Court's formula uses.
errors.source: The Court's cell, page 93, row Calculations - BTG Costing: 'BTG Cost = (Bottle List Price/25oz/750ml) * oz/ml pour'

notes: Mapped questions: Village 28 (Business of the Sommelier); no Régionale cat is mapped. Business stems outside the map: Service & Hospitality c-1ksexqiu, c-4gw8zkb1, c-eg0a7xci and c-bj2f7v48 (FIFO), Wine Trade & Aging c-96upusir (OWC) and c-yqxiozm7, Label Reading i-rd46oyl2, Tasting & Service i-9qt2ohue, Sweet Wines c-ametc74t. Of the Court's 11 rows, 9 have a chapter fact or a stem; the two Calculation - Combinations rows (pour cost from a case, bottles for an event) have neither, since every costing stem starts from a single bottle. The Village cat is pitched at the trade (stock turns, working capital, laddering, anchoring, allocations) and is thin on the Court's own mechanics: it never works in ounces, never names the 9 litre case, the litre, the 187 ml or the jeroboam, and never asks how many bottles an event needs. Court cells to read with care in our own copy: the Gross Profit cell is printed backwards, bottle cost minus list price (gross profit is list price minus bottle cost, as c-j1zp2eyy teaches), so an e- question keys the right way round and never quotes the cell as a formula; the BTG cell divides a list price, not a cost, and calls the result a cost; the bottles formula divides by 25, which holds only for a pour in ounces (in millilitres divide by 750); 'Jeroboam' is unqualified and is 3 litres in Champagne and Burgundy but 5 litres in Bordeaux (4.5 in older bottlings), as the bottles table says. No law or classification governs these rows; no search was spent.
